case.case_title: Tilak Karunaratne v. Mrs. Sirimavo Bandaranaike and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC (Spl.) 3/93, decided on 3 August 1993

clause.text: Freedom of speech and expression including publication.

case_context.legal_issue: To what extent can freedom of speech be restricted by the requirement of party discipline in the context of a political party member's public criticism of the party leadership?
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that his statement to the media criticizing the lack of democracy and non-holding of elections within the party was an exercise of his constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a).
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the petitioner breached party discipline by publicly criticizing internal party matters, and that such conduct justified his expulsion. They argued that freedom of speech is subject to limitations imposed by party discipline.
key_facts: Petitioner was a Member of Parliament and member of the Sri Lanka Freedom Party (SLFP).
Petitioner persistently urged party leadership to hold intra-party elections, which had not been held since 1986.
Petitioner gave a public interview to 'Lakdiva' newspaper on 24.01.1993 criticizing the party leadership and lack of democracy.
Petitioner was expelled from the party following a disciplinary inquiry which he refused to attend.
The Supreme Court had to determine the validity of the expulsion in light of constitutional freedoms.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court recognized that Article 14(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression, including publication, but this freedom is not absolute and can be limited by the requirements of party discipline inherent in the freedom of association under Article 14(1)(c). The court emphasized that political party membership involves contractual obligations, including self-limitation on speech to maintain party cohesion.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The petitioner had exhausted internal party forums to express his views but was denied opportunity due to non-convening of meetings and leadership resistance. His public statement was moderate, focused on the lack of democracy and non-holding of elections within the party, and was made in the interest of the party. The court found that in these circumstances, the petitioner's statement was justified as an exercise of his constitutional freedom of speech.
principles_established: Freedom of speech under Article 14(1)(a) is subject to reasonable limitations imposed by party discipline under Article 14(1)(c).
Political party membership entails contractual obligations including self-limitation on speech to preserve party unity.
A member's public criticism of the party may be justified if internal forums are unavailable or ineffective.
Expulsion for exercising constitutional freedom of speech in good faith and in the party's interest is invalid.
precedents_cited: Yapa Abeywardena v. Harsha Abeywardene and another
Dissanayake and Others v. Kaleel and Others

outcome.holding: The court held that the petitioner's public statement was a justified exercise of his freedom of speech under Article 14(1)(a) and that his expulsion on that ground was invalid.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The expulsion of the petitioner from the SLFP was declared invalid.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 14(1)(a) is central to the court's reasoning as the petitioner’s right to freedom of speech and expression was the constitutional basis for challenging the validity of his expulsion from the party.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner took every possible step within the party fora to persuade the party leadership to hold elections and when his persistent pleas brought no results, in the interest of the party he spoke to the media. The statement to 'Lakdiva' was couched in moderate language and was expressed without any semblance of vituperation directed at any person. The court held that in those circumstances the petitioner's impugned statements are justified as having been made in the exercise of his freedom of speech guaranteed under the Constitution.
